title: The Processor's Endless Loop
objective: After this level you can explain the fetch, decode and execute cycle a processor repeats billions of times a second.
summary: A processor fetches the instruction its program counter points to, decodes it, executes it and repeats, paced by a clock ticking billions of times a second.

cards.headline: Your processor knows one routine. It runs it billions of times a second.
cards.body: Every app, game and photo filter comes down to the same three steps, repeated without a break: get an instruction, work out what it means, do it. This is the loop at the heart of the machine.

cards.headline: Fetch, decode, execute
cards.body: The processor keeps a program counter: the memory address of the next instruction. Fetch: it collects the instruction stored at that address. Decode: it splits the instruction's binary pattern into parts, each with a meaning, such as 'add' and which numbers to add. Execute: it carries out the operation, perhaps sending two numbers through Level 7's adders.

cards.headline: Then again, and again
cards.body: After each fetch, the program counter usually steps on to the next instruction, so the processor works through a program in order. Some instructions, called jumps and branches, change the counter to point somewhere else, which lets a program go back and repeat or skip ahead. When one instruction is done, the cycle simply starts over.

cards.fact: A 3.2 GHz processor runs 3.2 billion clock cycles every second.
cards.context: A clock sends out pulses at a fixed, precise rate, and those pulses keep the fetch, decode and execute steps in time. Gigahertz means billions of cycles per second. On every single cycle, billions of transistors inside the processor open and close.

cards.headline: The loop: running

questions.prompt: What does a clock speed of 3.2 GHz mean?

options.label: 3.2 million instructions stored in memory
options.rationale: Gigahertz counts cycles per second, not stored instructions.

options.label: 3.2 gigabytes of memory
options.rationale: GB measures size; GHz measures cycles per second.

options.label: 3.2 programs running at once
options.rationale: It counts clock cycles, not programs.

questions.explanation: Gigahertz means billions of cycles per second: 3.2 GHz is 3.2 billion.

questions.prompt: How can a program go back and repeat a step it already ran?

options.label: The clock runs backward for a moment
options.rationale: The clock only ticks forward at a fixed rate.

options.label: The processor fetches the whole program again from storage
options.rationale: It just changes where the next fetch comes from.

options.label: A jump instruction changes the program counter to an earlier address
The decode step reads the instruction twice
options.rationale: Decoding splits one instruction into its parts.

questions.explanation: Jumps and branches change the program counter, so the next fetch comes from a different address.

questions.prompt: An add instruction reaches the execute step. Which circuits from Level 7 actually do the sum?

options.label: A chain of full adders built from gates
The program counter
options.rationale: It only points to the next instruction.

options.label: The clock
options.rationale: The clock paces the cycle; it does not add.

options.label: The camera sensor
options.rationale: The sensor turns light into numbers.

questions.explanation: The arithmetic-logic unit adds with gates wired into adders, each passing its carry along.
